messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 53
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Oceania
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Photographer
- Trauma Type: Captivity
- Pcl5: 62

He is 53, a photographer who has spent most of his adult life moving toward places other people avoid. Before everything changed, he describes himself as patient, observant, and good at disappearing behind the camera. He is married, and for years his work has taken him across the Pacific and beyond, photographing storms, political unrest, and remote communities. He says he always believed the camera gave him a kind of protection. If he could frame what was happening, he could survive it.

Several years ago, while traveling for an assignment, he is taken captive by an armed group after a vehicle checkpoint turns violent. He remembers the beginning in fragments that remain unnaturally vivid: the smell of diesel, someone shouting in a language he only partly understands, the hot pressure of hands forcing him to the ground, his cheek pressed into dirt. After that, time becomes confused. He is held in a small room for days, then weeks. He is blindfolded often enough that even now darkness against his face makes his chest seize. He is fed irregularly, threatened unpredictably, and made to listen for footsteps outside the door, never knowing whether someone is coming in to question him, hit him, or simply leave him alone with his own thoughts.

What stays with him most is not one dramatic moment but the slow erasure of ordinary life. He loses his sense of date and season. He starts measuring time by sounds: a bucket dragged down a hallway, a generator kicking on, the call of birds in the morning. At first he tries to keep himself intact by mentally composing photographs. He imagines aperture settings, light angles, contact sheets from old assignments. Eventually even that begins to fail. He becomes certain, then uncertain, then certain again that he will die there. He thinks often of his wife, picturing her making coffee in their kitchen at dawn, and then he stops letting himself picture her because it hurts too much.

When he is finally released, he expects relief to arrive cleanly. Instead, he says, freedom feels unreal. On the flight home he cannot sleep because every time his eyes close he sees the room again. Back in his own house, he startles at doors closing, at the hum of the refrigerator, at his wife touching his shoulder from behind. He begins checking locks repeatedly before bed, then checking the windows, then standing in the hallway listening for sounds that do not belong. His wife tells him he is home; he says he knows that, but his body does not.

He returns to photography because it is the only life he recognizes, but work has changed. Looking through the viewfinder now feels dangerous, as if narrowing his field of vision leaves him exposed. Crowds are nearly unbearable. At public events he positions himself with his back to walls and scans exits before he takes a single photo. If someone approaches too quickly, his whole body tenses. He has abandoned more than one assignment because the noise of a generator, a damp concrete room, or a strip of cloth brushing his face sends him somewhere else entirely. He does not think of these moments as memories at first. They feel present, total, as if captivity is happening again and everyone around him has failed to notice.

At home, his wife has learned the geography of his avoidance. He no longer goes into small windowless spaces. He refuses overseas jobs that once would have excited him, especially if travel involves unstable regions or armed escorts. He used to develop images in a darkroom for pleasure; now he cannot tolerate enclosed darkness and leaves the door open, flooding the room with light. He sleeps lightly, if at all. On bad nights he jerks awake sweating, convinced he has heard boots outside the bedroom door. His wife says he shouts in his sleep, sometimes begging, sometimes giving clipped answers as though being interrogated.

He speaks about captivity sparingly, but it intrudes everywhere. He feels ashamed of how afraid he is, ashamed that he survived by complying, ashamed that part of him remained emotionally absent even after he came home. He is quicker to anger than he used to be, especially when he feels cornered or controlled. Then just as quickly he withdraws. Friends have mostly stopped calling because he declines invitations, leaves gatherings early, or seems distant even when he attends. He says people want the version of the story where he was released and returned to normal. He cannot give them that.

What he can describe, sitting in the office now, is a life divided into before and after. He still takes photographs, though less often, and sometimes he notices that when the light is right, when he is alone near the sea, he can disappear into the work for a few minutes at a time. But even then he remains alert to sound, to movement, to the possibility of being trapped. He says captivity ended years ago, yet some part of him is still there, counting footsteps outside a door, waiting to learn what comes next.
